messages.content: What is the central limit theorem and why does it matter?

Central Limit Theorem (CLT): regardless of the underlying distribution's shape, the distribution of sample means approaches a normal distribution as sample size increases (typically n≥30 is sufficient). Why it matters: it justifies using normal distribution-based statistical tests (t-tests, z-tests) on real-world data that isn't normally distributed. It explains why the normal distribution appears everywhere in nature — many natural phenomena are the sum of many small independent effects. It enables confidence intervals and hypothesis testing — the foundation of scientific inference. Without CLT, we would need different statistical methods for every differently-distributed variable.
What is Bayes' theorem and how do you use it in real-world problems?

P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B). Example: disease prevalence 1% (prior P(disease)=0.01). Test: 99% sensitivity (P(positive|disease)=0.99), 99% specificity (P(negative|no disease)=0.99, so P(positive|no disease)=0.01). Positive test: P(disease|positive) = 0.99×0.01 / (0.99×0.01 + 0.01×0.99) = 0.0099/0.0198 = 50%. Counterintuitive: despite a highly accurate test, half of positives are false positives when the disease is rare. Application: any diagnostic or decision situation where you're updating belief based on evidence. The prior matters enormously — ignoring it leads to systematically wrong probability estimates. Bayesian reasoning is the formal version of updating beliefs proportionally to evidence.
What is the difference between Type I and Type II errors?

Type I error (false positive): rejecting the null hypothesis when it's actually true. Concluding an effect exists when it doesn't. Controlled by the significance level (α) — typically 0.05 means 5% chance of Type I error. Type II error (false negative): failing to reject the null hypothesis when it's actually false. Missing a real effect. Controlled by statistical power (1-β) — typically 80% power means 20% chance of Type II error. The trade-off: decreasing α (reducing Type I errors) increases β (more Type II errors). Increasing sample size reduces both. Context determines which error is more costly — medical screening prioritises low Type II (miss no true cases); criminal justice prioritises low Type I (convict no innocent people).
What is the Monte Carlo method and when do you use it?

Monte Carlo: using random sampling to estimate quantities that are analytically intractable. Process: define the problem mathematically, run thousands or millions of random trials according to the probability distributions of inputs, aggregate the results. Examples: estimating π (randomly throw darts at a unit square, the fraction inside the unit circle approximates π/4), portfolio risk estimation (simulate thousands of market scenarios, observe distribution of outcomes), option pricing (Black-Scholes has a closed form, but exotic options require Monte Carlo), project timeline estimation (sample from probability distributions for each task duration, simulate thousands of projects). The accuracy improves with √n trials — 100x more trials gives 10x more accuracy. Computationally expensive but universally applicable.
How do you interpret a confidence interval correctly?

A 95% confidence interval does NOT mean 'there is a 95% probability the true value is in this interval.' The true value is fixed — it's either in the interval or it isn't. Correct interpretation: if we repeated this study 100 times with different samples, approximately 95 of the resulting intervals would contain the true value. Practically: a wider interval reflects less precision (smaller sample or more variable data). A 95% CI that doesn't include zero for a difference means the effect is statistically significant at α=0.05. Common misinterpretation: treating the CI as a probability statement about the true value — that's the Bayesian credible interval, not the frequentist CI.
